A.explanation: Combines $u_1 - u_2$ with $v_2 + v_1$, which does not give the speed of approach or the speed of separation for the directions shown.

B.explanation: Uses $u_1 - u_2$ for approach, but the spheres move towards each other before collision so their relative speed is the sum $u_1 + u_2$.

C.explanation: Uses $v_2 + v_1$ for separation, but both spheres move to the right after collision so their separation speed is the difference $v_2 - v_1$.

D.explanation: Speed of approach $u_1 + u_2$ equals speed of separation $v_2 - v_1$ for a perfectly elastic collision along one line.

hints: Notice the arrow directions: before collision $u_1$ points right and $u_2$ points left, while after collision both $v_1$ and $v_2$ point right.
Recall that for a perfectly elastic collision the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation along the line of impact.
Work out approach speed from $u_1$ and $u_2$ moving towards each other, and separation speed from $v_1$ and $v_2$ both moving the same way with the right-hand sphere ahead.
walkthrough: Before collision the left sphere moves right with speed $u_1$ and the right sphere moves left with speed $u_2$, so they are closing the gap from both sides.
Speed of approach is therefore the sum: $u_1 + u_2$.
After collision both spheres move to the right, with the right-hand sphere with speed $v_2$ ahead of the left-hand sphere with speed $v_1$.
Speed of separation is how fast the ahead sphere pulls away from the behind sphere: $v_2 - v_1$.
For a perfectly elastic head-on collision, relative speed is conserved: speed of approach = speed of separation.
Hence $u_1 + u_2 = v_2 - v_1$. This is option D.
